metadata.title: Clinical Guideline for the treatment of SCLERITIS AND EPISCLERITIS
metadata.summary: This guideline covers the clinical assessment, investigation, treatment and follow-up of episcleritis and scleritis, including necrotising and posterior presentations. It distinguishes care by severity, addresses suspected infection and associated systemic disease, and describes when specialist review or admission is needed.

Assess risk factors for atypical scleritis, including infection, masquerade conditions such as MM, and prior surgery or trauma.

In the subspecialty clinic, carry out a systemic assessment using blood tests, urinalysis and imaging.
Use oral NSAID as first-line treatment for episcleritis or mild scleritis, with or without FML or PF/Maxidex.
Consider a topical antibiotic when keratitis is also present.
Discuss moderate to severe scleritis with the registrar on-call.
If infection is suspected, treat the infectious cause before other treatment.

For moderate or severe scleritis, consult a senior ophthalmologist or the registrar on call and arrange a subspecialty clinic appointment within 1-2 weeks.
Consider whether a GP letter or referral is needed for underlying conditions.

document_sections.heading: DESCRIPTION
document_sections.content: Scleritis affects the deep episcleral vascular plexus and the sclera beneath it. Episcleritis affects the superficial episcleral vascular plexus and conjunctiva. Presentation is typically in middle age, with F>M. An underlying inflammatory disorder is present in 30%; RA, GPA and PAN are the most common.

document_sections.heading: RED FLAGS
document_sections.content: Scleritis or episcleritis may be the initial sign of serious systemic disease, making a review of systems and medical history important. An area of pale, avascular sclera is a warning sign of necrotising scleritis. Scleromalacia perforans is necrotising scleritis without inflammation; it is painless or asymptomatic, associated with RA, and involves chronic occlusive vasculitis.

document_sections.heading: HOW TO ASSESS HISTORY
document_sections.content: Ask about a red, painful eye, possible loss of vision, gradual symptom onset, previous ocular inflammation or infection, and associated medical conditions. Episcleritis generally causes no pain or only mild discomfort; scleritis causes moderate to severe pain that may wake the patient. Assess risk factors for atypical scleritis, including infection, masquerade conditions such as MM, and prior surgery or trauma.

document_sections.heading: EXAMINATION
document_sections.content: Begin examination in a brightly lit room without a slit lamp. Look for dilated episcleral and scleral vessels. Episcleral vessels readily blanch with phenylephrine, which can help distinguish episcleritis from scleritis. Scleritis may be nodular, diffuse or necrotising; pale or avascular scleral areas suggest the necrotising form. Check for scleral thinning, which appears grey or blue and is most apparent in diffuse light. Examine the cornea, anterior chamber and posterior chamber for inflammation, and assess IOP. Posterior scleritis can occur despite a white eye and may feature serous RD, macular oedema, disc oedema, choroidal thickening or folds; B Scan may show T-Sign.

document_sections.heading: INVESTIGATIONS
document_sections.content: Take a detailed history. At the first presentation, review systems to evaluate the possibility of underlying systemic disease. Obtain OCT or B-Scan when indicated, and swabs or scrapings if infection is suspected. Measure BP. A subspecialty clinic should undertake systemic evaluation with blood tests, urinalysis and imaging.

document_sections.heading: TREATMENT
document_sections.content: For episcleritis or mild scleritis, first-line treatment is oral NSAID, with or without FML or PF/Maxidex. Consider topical antibiotic cover when keratitis is associated. Discuss moderate to severe scleritis with the on-call registrar. If an infectious cause is suspected, treat it first. Oral steroid starts at 60mg, with PPI and optionally calcichew. Admit severe cases for intravenous methylprednisolone.

document_sections.heading: FOLLOW-UP
document_sections.content: Mild or moderate episcleritis is often self-limiting; discharge with treatment and advice. For severe episcleritis or mild scleritis, arrange one EED follow-up within 1 week and refer to a subspecialty clinic if the condition is not resolving. For moderate or severe scleritis, discuss the case with a senior ophthalmologist or the on-call registrar and arrange a subspecialty clinic appointment within 1-2 weeks. Systemic immunosuppression is associated with reduced mortality in scleritis. Consider whether a GP letter or referral is needed for underlying conditions.

artifacts.title: DESCRIPTION

columns:
DESCRIPTION

• Scleritis - inflammation of the deep vascular plexus of episclera and underlying sclera
• Episcleritis – inflammation of the superficial episcleral vascular plexus and conjunctiva
• Typically presents in middle age, F>M
• 30% with underlying inflammatory disorder (RA, GPA and PAN most common)

artifacts.summary: Defines the tissues affected by scleritis and episcleritis and notes their typical presentation and association with inflammatory disorders.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Distinguishing the affected tissues helps differentiate the conditions, while the systemic association informs clinical assessment.

artifacts.title: RED FLAGS

columns:
RED FLAGS

• Can be first presentation of serious systemic illness – NB systems review and Hx
• Beware necrotising scleritis – presents as an area of blanched/avascular sclera
• Scleromalacia perforans (necrotising scleritis without inflammation) is painless/asymptomatic, RA associated, chronic occlusive vasculitis

artifacts.description: The source places the heading and its warning signs in one table cell, with no separate data rows.
artifacts.summary: Identifies possible systemic disease and the appearances of necrotising scleritis and Scleromalacia perforans as important warnings.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: These findings prompt attention to potentially serious systemic illness and to necrotising disease that may lack pain.

artifacts.title: HOW TO ASSESS HISTORY

columns:
HOW TO ASSESS HISTORY

• Red, painful eye
• Possible vision loss
• Gradual onset
• Prior history of ocular inflammation/infection
• Prior history of associated medical conditions
• Episcleritis typically painless or mild discomfort, scleritis moderate to severe pain, can wake patient from sleep
• Assess relevant risk factors for atypical scleritis – infectious, masquerade (e.g. MM) and post-surgery/trauma

artifacts.description: The history prompts appear together with their heading in a single table cell; there are no distinct data rows.
artifacts.summary: Lists symptoms, prior ocular and medical history, differences in pain, and risk factors for atypical scleritis.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The history helps distinguish episcleritis from scleritis and identify presentations requiring assessment for other causes.

artifacts.title: EXAMINATION AND INVESTIGATIONS

columns:
EXAMINATION

• Examine at first in brightly lit room, without slit lamp
• Dilated episcleral and scleral vessels
• Episcleral vessels blanch readily with phenylephrine, can help differentiate scleritis and episcleritis
• Scleritis can be nodular, diffuse or necrotising
• Blanched or avascular areas indicate necrotising scleritis
• Assess for thinning of sclera – appears grey/blue, best noted with diffuse light
• Assess remaining eye for inflammation – cornea, anterior chamber, and posterior chamber
• IOP
• Posterior scleritis may have serous RD, macular oedema, disc oedema, choroidal thickening/folds, B Scan may show T-Sign, can occur with a white eye.


INVESTIGATIONS

• Detailed history NB
• If first presentation, systems review to assess risk of underlying systemic disease
• OCT, B-Scan if indicated
• Swabs/scrapings if infectious cause suspected
• BP
• Systemic evaluation with bloods, urinalysis, and imaging in subspecialty clinic.

artifacts.summary: Sets out ocular examination findings and investigations for suspected scleritis or episcleritis, including assessment for posterior, infectious, and systemic disease.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The findings and tests guide differentiation between the conditions and recognition of necrotising or posterior scleritis.

artifacts.title: TREATMENT

columns:
TREATMENT

• First line treatment for episcleritis/mild scleritis is oral NSAID +/- FML or PF/Maxidex.
• Consider cover with topical antibiotic if associated keratitis.
• Moderate to severe scleritis should be discussed with the registrar on-call.
• Infectious cause must be treated first if suspected.
• Oral steroid starting at 60mg (with PPI +/- calcichew).
• Admission for intravenous methylprednisolone with severe cases.

artifacts.description: All treatment points share one table cell with the heading; the source has no separate regimen rows.
artifacts.summary: Presents treatment by severity, consideration of associated keratitis, the priority of treating suspected infection, and escalation for severe cases.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It links treatment choices and escalation to disease severity while preserving the requirement to treat a suspected infectious cause first.

artifacts.title: FOLLOW-UP

columns:
FOLLOW-UP

• Mild/moderate episcleritis – often self-limiting, discharge with treatment and advice.
• Severe episcleritis/mild scleritis – follow up once in EED within 1 week, if not resolving refer to subspecialty clinic.
• Moderate/severe scleritis – discuss with senior ophthalmologist or registrar on call and book subspecialty clinic within 1-2 weeks.
• Systemic immunosuppression associated with reduced mortality in scleritis
• Consider need for GP letter or referral re underlying conditions.
